newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cargill thinks gene beans already in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Cargill thinks gene beans already in Europe.

text.p: Commodity trading giant Cargill said Tuesday that the first exports to Europe of genetically altered U.S. soybeans probably arrived at its Amsterdam plant 10 days ago and had already been processed and delivered to customers.
Protests by European environmentalists gathered pace this week against the start of sales by the United States of soybeans that have been genetically changed to withstand treatment with a weedkiller.

A spokesman for the Dutch arm of Cargill, a U.S. trading house, cited a cargo of beans that was delivered from an unspecified North American port on the freighter Amber, which arrived Nov. 2, to be crushed in the normal way in a process that takes only a few hours.
"The modified beans could well have been in the shipment. The problem is that you just can't tell them apart," he said.
Between 1 percent and 2 percent of U.S. soybean exports are now expected to contain modified beans, developed by Monsanto Co. to be resistant to its Roundup weedkiller.
The Cargill spokesman said the firm's position on handling the new beans had not changed despite recent blockades of European ports by the environmental group Greenpeace.
"Our policy has always been that we do not transport beans that have not been properly tested," he said.
Cargill believed the new beans to be totally safe and the spokesman also cited regulatory approval of them by U.S. and European medical authorities.
Greenpeace calls the beans a hazardous experiment with nature.

Protest gathered momentum Monday when activists occupied the office of Austrian Health Minister Christa Krammer. In Vevey, Switzerland, police dispersed others who staged a roof protest at the headquarters of Nestle, the world's biggest food company.
Nestle said it was satisfied the soybeans were safe. "We are singularly unimpressed with the scientific evidence presented by Greenpeace," spokesman Francois Perroud said.
Greenpeace has also protested at Hamburg and Antwerp in attempts to stop beans being delivered at these ports.
The Cargill spokesman said that in the context of overall demand for meal and vegetable oil, there had been very little impact from the issue. Prices were yet to be affected, he said.
Some European food firms, including Unilever's unit in Germany, where consumer fears are among the most widespread, have pledged not to use the beans, even though they consider them safe.
